messages.author: 5900eadecec2d82d
messages.subject: Re: Ungulate data set
parts:
Kausik,

Here's how I'd do it:

Put a field (column) in the observation data layer called "species". Then,
for each observation, you put the species code in this column, along with
the distances in the Perp distance column, the cluster size in the Cluster
size column, etc.

Now, to analyze data for just one species, create a new analysis, and a new
data filter for that analysis, and then in the Data selection tab of the
Data Filter Properties, click on "+" to add a new selection criterion, and
under "Layer Type" choose observation and under "Selection criteria" type
something like
Species = "Elephant"
or whatever species code it is you want to select out.

You can set up one data filter for each species you want to analyze, and use
this data filter for lots of analyses on this species using, for example,
different model definitions that define alternative detection function
models.

There are several ways you could approach the analysis for all ungulates.

The easiest, but probably not the best, is to run an analysis of all the
data pooled - that is with no data filter selection criteria. This should
give you a more-or-less unbiased estiamte of total density - you're relying
on the pooling robustness property of the detection function estimator,
which means there should be little bias in the overall density estimate even
if you pool together groups (in this case species) with rather different
detection functions.

If the animals do have very different detection functions, the above will
not work (you will get bad bias). Also, precision might be poor. So, a
second approach (if you have enough data) would be to post-stratify by
species, or use species as a covariate in an MCDS analysis.

The only downside of this is that you might already in your previous by-
species analyses, have selected different key functions (+ adjustments) for
the different species, and perhaps you want to keep this in the combined
analysis. If so, the only way I can think of is to manually sum the
densities from each of the by-species analyses done previously.
Unfortunately, to get a variance estimate, some hand calculations are then
required, as outlined in sections 3.6.1 and 3.7.1 of Introduction to
Distance Sampling. If the thought of some hand-calculating seems too much,
then possible stick with one of the strategies outlined in the previous 2
paragraphs instead!

Hope this helps,

- Len Thomas
